 USDA proposal could cut SNAP benefits for 6.3 million people 
 Americans who rely on food stamps could soon lose their benefits. By Gabriela Johnson Published : Nov. 10, 2026 at 10:37 PM CST | Updated : 3 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google MONTGOMERY, Ala. ( WSFA ) - The Trump administration has proposed a rule that could cut SNAP benefits for about 6.3 million people, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
 The USDA proposal , released Monday, would limit automatic SNAP eligibility to households that receive cash assistance through the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program, known as TANF. Households receiving noncash or nominal TANF services would no longer automatically qualify and would have to meet SNAP income and asset limits.
 What the proposal targets
 The proposal targets a policy known as “broad-based categorical eligibility.” The policy lets states use TANF benefits such as child care or workforce training to qualify households for SNAP without applying the program’s standard income limit.
 The USDA estimates nearly 18% of SNAP recipients, or about 6.3 million people, would lose benefits under the change. The agency also estimates 1.8 million children would lose eligibility for free school lunches.
 According to the proposal, the change would save $44.6 billion between 2027 and 2031. It is the administration’s latest effort to curb SNAP spending, citing concerns about waste and fraud. The rule says the change would make SNAP eligibility more standardized and “preserve benefits for the truly needy.”
 Alabama Arise responds
 Carol Gundlach, senior policy analyst for Alabama Arise, a nonprofit that speaks on behalf of Alabamians who live in poverty, said the proposal is part of a broader effort to reduce eligibility.
 “What they’re doing is they’re whittling away eligibility to get SNAP food assistance every way they can figure out,” Gundlach said.
 Advocates for the poor call the SNAP income limits outdated. Gundlach said ending broad-based categorical eligibility would also bring back asset tests, requiring caseworkers to spend time verifying a family’s valuable property.
 “The more stuff you have to verify, the more likely there is to make a mistake – and that drives up our error rate and the money we have to spend just to run the SNAP program,” Gundlach said.
 Gundlach also said losing SNAP recipients would affect school meals.
 “The more people we lose from food assistance, the fewer kids are eligible automatically to get free meals at school,” she said.
 “We knew this was coming, because the current administration is at war with public assistance programs and the people who get them,” Gundlach said. “We’re going to do everything we can do to stop that.”
 Public comment period
 The public has 30 days to comment on the proposed rule before the USDA moves forward. The rule remains a proposal. After the comment period, the USDA can revise it, delay it or move ahead with a final version.
 Gundlach said she is attending a national meeting of SNAP advocates from every state in Albuquerque, and that the proposed rule will be a topic of discussion. She said advocates, lawyers and national organizations will submit comments asking the USDA to withdraw the proposed change. She said she expects the rule to be litigated.
 “Anybody can comment on a proposed regulation. The more comments they get, the longer it takes to implement a rule because they have to consider every single comment,” Gundlach said. “We want everybody that is concerned about this to submit a comment.”
 How to submit a comment
 Online: Go to regulations.gov and follow the instructions for submitting comments. 
 Mail: SNAP Program Development Division, Food and Nutrition Administration, 5601 Sunnyside Ave, Beltsville, MD 20705 
 Email: sm.fn.snappdbrules@usda.gov. Include Docket ID Number FNA-2026-0661, “Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility” in the subject line.
